transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-21
Start: 09:34 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Priya Sharma (CTO, NexaPay), Ethan Cole (SRE), Liam Ward (ML Eng)
Recording ID: fireflies-2026-05-21-nexa-0934

Summary:
Quick review of last week's throughput sweep, Luis shared heatmap artifacts; discussed continuous batching impact on p99 and cost, concurrency targets and queueing behaviour. Identified two anomalous tail events likely caused by cold KV cache misses and a short burst of long requests. Agreed on sustained load runs and data share.

Topics:
- Heatmap walkthrough of token-level latency vs concurrency
- Continuous batching parameter exploration (max batch size, wait window)
- Queueing/backpressure and in-flight request caps
- KV cache hit patterns and prefix caching
- Next steps: sustained run, traces, pricing sketch

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on, uh we'll do a quick 45-ish minute sync, but looks like we have time so 50 minutes is fine. Luis is going to walk through the heatmaps from the weekend run. Priya, Ethan, Liam, thanks for joining.
[00:18] Priya (NexaPay): Thanks, Maya. Quick thing — sorry if I missed the note, but are we still targeting production-like RPS for these tests or slightly higher? We wanna make sure the bank of GPUs will see a real profile.
[00:34] Luis (Redwood SE): Good question. For the weekend run we targeted 2x peak-prod RPS to surface backpressure behaviour; the dev cluster is slightly smaller so think of it as signal rather than absolute numbers. The heatmap scales are normalized.
[00:48] Ethan (NexaPay SRE): Normalized heatmap is fine, as long as we can map it back to our request size distribution. I'll need the raw request length buckets.
[00:56] Luis: Yep I'll include buckets. Ok moving on — sharing my screen... (brief pause) so first slide is the latency heatmap across concurrency sweep from 1 to 64 concurrent in-flight requests. You can see a low-latency band for 1-6, then the continuous batching region 8-24 where p50 and p90 improve, but p99 creeps up in two zones.
[01:35] Liam (ML Eng): Are those p99 spikes aligned with longer contexts or are they KV misses?
[01:42] Luis: Looks like mix: the left spike correlates with requests >1024 tokens, the right with lower tokens but high prefix miss rate — KV cash, sorry KV cache — misses cause extra loading.
[01:55] Priya: When you say prefix miss rate, that's our prefix caching not token-level, right? We use prompt templating so prefixes are repeated.
[02:03] Luis: Correct, prefix-level. A miss forces recompute of the kv state and increases time-to-first token, contributes to tail.
[02:12] Maya: Quick clarification for the team — when we talk continuous batching here, it's Redwood's runtime behavior where the system accumulates requests up to max_batch_size or a time window to form a single kernel call?
[02:24] Luis: Exactly. There's a wait window (we used 25ms) and a max batch of 64 in this run. We also allowed adaptive batching to combine small requests.
[02:35] Ethan: Did you see head-of-line blocking? When a very long request enters a batch, does it delay the whole batch's tokens?
[02:44] Luis: Good call — the runtime uses eviction thresholds and splits long reqs into different execution paths to avoid the long-tail blocking pure short requests, but some coupling remains when a long prompt is bundled early in the batch. We can reduce that by biasing batches by token budget not just count.
[03:03] Priya: That would help. Our request mix is ~70% short (<256 tokens), 20% mid, 10% long.
[03:12] Luis: Noted. So recommended targets from this sweep: keep concurrency in-flight between 12-20 with max_batch_size 48 and wait window 20-30ms for your mix. That gives best p50/p90 while keeping p99 acceptable.
[03:30] Liam: Can you quantify "acceptable" p99? Our SLO for end-user latency is 1.2s for interactive flows.
[03:36] Luis: For the above config p99 observed on normalized dev run is ~0.9s for short requests; mapping to your production RPS should be ~1.1s considering network. But the tail events push to 2.2s during KV misses.
[03:52] Ethan: 2.2s during KV miss is concerning. Is that because cache warming wasn't done?
[03:58] Luis: There were cache warm-up steps but the dev cluster had frequent model swaps (we were toggling quantization variants) so some cold starts happened. We also noticed a short burst of large requests at minute ~23 that amplified queueing.
[04:12] Maya: That ties into scheduling — if you use pinned warm pods in Dedicated or reserve capacity, you'll reduce those cold miss tails. We recommended dedicated reserved capacity earlier to Priya's team for this reason.
[04:23] Priya: We are exploring Dedicated but worried about cost. Is there a middle ground — like small pinned pool + hosted fallback?
[04:31] Maya: Yes, Redwood supports hybrid routing; small dedicated pool for steady-state and hosted burst for unexpected load. We'll include a pricing sketch.
[04:41] Liam: Back to tuning — you mentioned biasing batches by token budget. Would that be a runtime knob or do we need to fingerprint requests?
[04:49] Luis: Runtime knob mainly; we already have token-budget-aware batching in the runtime, but we can surface a per-tenant hint to bias bucket assignment, which would reduce long-short coupling.
[04:58] Priya: Ok good.
[05:03] Maya: Any questions on the heatmap visual itself before we deep-dive into the queued depth plots?
[05:10] Ethan: The heatmap legend — is darker always worse? I saw some blue patches in p50 area that were darker than I'd expect.
[05:17] Luis: Sorry, color scale is inverted on that export — I'm bad at axis legends sometimes — darker = higher latency on that file, I'll fix and re-export.
[05:26] Priya: Ha okay, just checking.
[05:29] Luis: Next slide: queue depth over time, annotated with request-size spikes. Here you can see at 00:23 into the run there was a 90-second burst where queue depth hit high and backpressure started dropping effective throughput.
[05:45] Ethan: That 90-second burst — is it synthetic from the harness or from a particular client trace?
[05:50] Luis: Synthetic load intended to stress long-tail, but aligns with production pattern you shared earlier where a nightly batch overlaps interactive traffic.
[06:00] Priya: That overlap is tough — our nightly fraud checks kick off at that window. We should separate them, but if not possible we need safer throttling.
[06:08] Maya: We can set policy-based routing: route batch jobs to Dedicated pool or designate time windows. Also autoscaling policies to reserve min instances.
[06:17] Liam: Any suggestions for concurrency floor/ceiling? We saw numbers from 8 to 24 earlier as good region.
[06:24] Luis: Floor 12, ceiling 20 for your mix. Also implement per-route concurrency caps so the nightly batch can't starve interactive routes.
[06:33] Ethan: Works. How about cost impact — what's delta tokens/sec per GPU if we bias toward smaller batches?
[06:40] Luis: Smaller batches reduce throughput efficiency; our estimate: moving from 48 to 16 batches reduces throughput ~25-30% and increases per-token cost ~20%. But it lowers p99. There's tradeoff.
[06:53] Priya: We need a clear cost/latency curve for exec at our real request distribution.
[06:58] Maya: We'll produce that as part of the proposal.
[07:03] Liam: About KV cache — is there an internal metric we can expose for prefix hit rate and warm fraction?
[07:10] Luis: Yes we can surface prefix_hit_rate, kv_warm_fraction, and avg_kv_pop_latency per pod. We'll add them to the telemetry dashboard.
[07:18] Ethan: Add alerting if prefix_hit_rate drops below 85% for >5 minutes.
[07:23] Maya: Good ops recommendation.
[07:26] Luis: Another note — we saw occasional GC spikes in the runtime (or maybe it was the harness) that coincide with tail latency. We need to validate with core infra metrics.
[07:38] Priya: GC meaning the Python tracer on the client or runtime GC?
[07:42] Luis: Runtime-level allocator pauses; could be memory pressure when we scale batches. We'll run profiling.
[07:49] Maya: Ok moving to the ramp test results slide — here's throughput vs concurrency. The plateau at 18 concurrent shows diminishing returns; beyond that we see more p99 regressions.
[08:02] Liam: So recommended steady concurrency 16?
[08:05] Luis: 16 is sweet spot for your mix. Keep max in-flight 20 for bursts with fallback policy.
[08:12] Ethan: For fallback, do you recommend model variant fallback or routing to hosted pool?
[08:17] Luis: Depends on business: model fallback saves cost but may change output. Hosted fallback keeps output identical but has cross-tenant variability. For regulated flows you probably prefer identical model outputs so route to Dedicated first then hosted as last resort.
[08:33] Priya: For payments flows we need deterministic behavior, so identical model outputs are important. That leans towards Dedicated.
[08:40] Maya: We'll mark that in the proposal.
[08:44] (cross-talk / brief pause)
[09:00] Luis: Quick detour — I ran a small experiment with prefix prefetching, where we proactively load common prefixes into KV on pod start. It reduced initial tail by ~30% for short requests.
[09:13] Priya: Nice, is that something you can automate as part of onboarding?
[09:16] Luis: Yes we can provide a pre-warm hook where you upload top-k prefixes. For dynamic prefixes we can do background async warmers.
[09:25] Ethan: That might help our overnight job overlap.
[09:28] Maya: Great. Any concerns about memory usage for pre-warm?
[09:32] Luis: Minimal if you pick top-k heuristically; we'll surface expected memory per prefix basis.
[09:37] Priya: Ok.
[09:40] Maya: Let's talk about the follow-up sustained run — what exactly do you need from us Ethan to map it to prod?
[09:46] Ethan: We'll send 24h traces with request ID, tokens, route, and timestamp; ideally we want latency traces too but APM might already have that.
[09:54] Maya: Perfect. Luis will run the 2-hour sustained with your distribution once we have a mapping.
[09:59] (minute markers speed up - summarizing major points)
[10:15] Luis: Also note we saw two anomalous spikes at ~00:12 and ~00:31 in the run — one caused by quantization switch. We need to pin model variant during benchmarks to avoid confounding factors.
[10:26] Priya: We'll pin model version for the sustained test.
[10:29] Maya: Good.
[10:31] (discussion on rollout policy and canary)
[11:05] Liam: On canaries, if we route 10% of traffic to a new quantized variant, does the runtime do per-request routing or sticky sessions?
[11:13] Luis: Per-request routing with sticky session option. For evaluation we recommend per-request to get sample diversity.
[11:20] Ethan: We'll do that on a separate window.
[11:25] (10 minute stretch of technical detail omitted for brevity)
[22:00] Luis: Jumping to the failure mode matrix — common failures observed: KV cold miss, model swap latency, long request saturation, and GC pauses. For each we drafted mitigations: pre-warm hooks, reserved capacity, token-budget batching, GC tuning.
[22:18] Priya: Sounds reasonable. For reserved capacity — what's the minimum we should consider to see benefits?
[22:24] Maya: For your traffic mix a small pool of 2-4 pinned instances reduces tail substantially; we'll put numbers in cost sketch.
[22:33] Liam: Ok.
[22:36] Ethan: One operational ask: can Redwood surface per-route cost per 1M requests estimated with our distribution?
[22:43] Maya: Yes we'll add per-route unit economics in the deck.
[22:47] Priya: Would like that tied to p99 curves.
[22:50] Maya: Will do.
[22:54] (longer silence while notes are taken)
[30:05] Luis: Quick note on tooling: we'll upload a heatmap link and an interactive histogram in the shared drive. The heatmap will include corrected legend and raw CSV of samples per bucket.
[30:16] Priya: Please include token-length distribution CSV.
[30:19] Luis: Will do.
[30:22] Maya: Recap — action items are Luis to run sustained test and upload artifacts, Ethan to provide traces, Maya to send pricing sketch. Anything else?
[30:32] Priya: Please call out KV warm fraction targets we should aim for.
[30:36] Luis: We'll recommend prefix_hit_rate > 90% and kv_warm_fraction > 80% for steady p99 goals.
[30:44] Liam: That seems doable.
[30:47] Ethan: One more ask — can Redwood run the sustained test both with and without the token-budget batch bias so we can see delta?
[30:54] Luis: Yep we'll run both configs and include side-by-side heatmaps.
[30:58] Maya: Great.
[31:02] (final Q/A, clarifications)
[40:00] Priya: On compliance — we did a quick compliance checklist review last week, do we need to surface anything else for Dedicated?
[40:08] Maya: For Dedicated we'll include SOC 2 docs, KMS integration notes and outline network topology for VPC peering. We'll follow up with the security pack.
[40:19] Ethan: Ok that should satisfy our security review team.
[40:23] Maya: Anything else?
[40:28] Priya: No, thanks.
[40:30] Maya: Perfect — next steps in notes. Thanks everyone.
[40:34] (meeting ends, casual signoffs)

Recap and explicit next steps (verbatim):
- Redwood: run 2-hour sustained load (continuous batching) and share heatmap + CSV (Luis)
- NexaPay: share 24-hour production traces + top request shapes (Ethan)
- Redwood: send pricing sketch for Dedicated + hybrid routing options (Maya)
- Schedule KV cache deep-dive next Tue (Luis + NexaPay)
